1:
The chapter opens on a peace suddenly shadowed, and the witnesses set the scene before they weigh the sin. The reformed John Gill fixes the moment by its "now when these things were done": Ezra and the returned captives had refreshed themselves, weighed out the money and the vessels into the hands of proper officers, offered their sacrifices, and delivered the king's commissions to his lieutenants and governors — and it was then, when all seemed settled, that the trouble broke. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke identifies the offenders precisely: they were not newcomers but the people who had returned long before with Zerubbabel and settled in Judea, whom Ezra on his arrival found "to be little better than the Canaanitish nations" from whom God had commanded Israel to keep separate.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch lay out the whole movement the verse begins. While Ezra was in the temple some time after his arrival, the princes of the people came to inform him that the Israelites had mingled themselves by marriage with the peoples of the lands; the report threw him into deep grief, so that he sat astonished until the evening sacrifice while all who feared God's word gathered about him, and at that sacrifice he fell upon his knees and made a touching confession of sin in the name of the congregation.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry probes what made the sin so grave. It was mingling with the people of the lands — associating in trade and conversation and, to complete the affinity, taking their daughters in marriage for their sons. He will hope they did not worship the strange gods, their captivity having cured them of idolatry; yet Bishop Patrick's reading of "they did according to their abominations" is that the very promiscuous marrying would by degrees lead them back to it. Herein, Henry says, they disobeyed the express command of Deut. 7:3; they profaned the crown of their peculiarity, levelling themselves with the nations God had dignified them above; they distrusted God's all-sufficiency, hoping by carnal policy to strengthen themselves among their neighbours — "a practical disbelief of God's all-sufficiency is at the bottom of all the sorry shifts we make"; and they exposed their children to the very idolatry that had once ruined church and nation. Worst of all, the offenders were not only unthinking people but priests and Levites whose office was to teach that law, and the hand of the princes and rulers, who should have prevented it, was "chief in this trespass" — and miserable, Henry adds, is the people whose leaders debauch them and cause them to err.
2:
The indictment grows specific: the returned exiles had taken of the daughters of the surrounding peoples for themselves and for their sons, so that "the holy seed have mingled themselves with the people of those lands." The reformed John Gill sorts out how widely the corruption spread. Some who were widowers had taken wives of these nations, whether while still in Babylon, where many such peoples also dwelt, or since their return; others took heathen daughters as wives for their sons; and some who already had wives took idolatrous ones besides. The sin, in other words, ran through every rank and condition of the community.

The phrase "the holy seed" carries the weight of the charge, and the grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch let the following action measure how deeply it wounded Ezra. When he heard it he rent both his garment and his mantle — the tearing of the upper and under garment being a sign of heartfelt and grievous affliction, as at Joshua 7:6 — and he plucked out a portion of the hair of his head and beard, which they distinguish carefully from the shorn head of ordinary mourning in Job 1:20: the plucking of the hair is rather the expression of violent wrath and moral indignation, the very gesture Nehemiah would use against this same sin in Nehemiah 13:25. Then he "sat down stunned" — the Hebrew word denoting one desolate, rigid, and motionless — while all who trembled at the word of God concerning the transgression of the exiles assembled about him.

Both the reformed Gill and the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fasten on the sting in the last clause — that "the hand of the princes and rulers hath been chief in this trespass." Clarke draws out its force: it was the first men, the most illustrious, who were the most capital offenders, and he reaches for Virgil's Aeneid, where one warrior hemmed within the walls is charged with plunging crowds of heroes to the shades below, to catch how the leaders' guilt outweighed the rest. The men who by rank and office should have been the surest guardians of the holy seed were foremost in defiling it, and so the shame of the whole community gathered upon its head. The witnesses do not divide; together they show a corruption that reached from the common household to the highest seats, and a scribe so overwhelmed by it that he could only sit down in silent horror.
3:
Ezra's grief takes bodily form, and the witnesses read each gesture as the language of a soul in anguish. The reformed John Gill notes that he rent both his garment and his mantle — the inner garment close to the body and the loose outer one thrown over it — a double token of the sorrow and mourning that so distressing a report had stirred. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sets the act in its wider world: this rending of the outer and inner garment in sign of great grief is frequently mentioned in the sacred writings and was common among all the ancient nations. But he lingers on the sharper sign — the plucking off of the hair. Shaving the head and beard were themselves marks of excessive grief; the plucking out of the hair, which must produce exquisite pain, went further still, testifying Ezra's abhorrence not merely of the act of taking strange wives but of the people's having joined them in their idolatrous abominations.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the impression the report made and finds in it a whole theology of holy sorrow. Ezra sat down astonished, Henry says, from a deep sense first of the dishonour done to God — it grieved him to the heart that a people called by God's name should so grossly violate his law, be so little bettered by his correction, and make such bad returns for his favours — and second of the mischief the people had done themselves and the danger they now stood in of God's wrath breaking out against them. From this Henry draws his notes: the sins of others should be our sorrow, and the injury they do to God's honour and to men's souls we should lay to heart; sorrow for sin must be great sorrow, such as Ezra's, mourning as for an only son or a firstborn; and the scandalous sins of professors are a thing we have reason to be astonished at. "We may stand amazed," he writes, "to see men contradict, disparage, prejudice, ruin themselves" — acting so inconsiderately and so inconsistently with themselves that upright men are astonished at it.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the plain meaning of the torn garments, Clarke the antiquity and severity of the self-inflicted pain, Henry the inward springs of a sorrow that reckons another's sin its own. Together they set before us a reformer who meets the discovery of hidden corruption not with a decree or a rebuke but with rent clothes, torn hair, and silent astonishment — the first and truest response of a man who feels the wound sin deals to God before ever he calculates the harm it does to men.
4:
Around the stricken scribe there forms a company of the like-minded, and the witnesses attend to who they were and why they came. The reformed John Gill describes them by their reverence: everyone that trembled at the words of the God of Israel — those who held his word in awe, feared to break his laws, and dreaded the judgments they knew must fall on transgressors — gathered themselves to Ezra. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch note the precise ground of their trembling: it was "because of the transgression of those that had been carried away," the sin of the returned exiles, that these God-fearers were terrified; and Ezra sat on, astonished, until the evening sacrifice.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fixes both the people and the hour. "Those that had been carried away" are again the returnees who had come up long before with Zerubbabel. And the evening sacrifice marks the time: as the morning sacrifice was the first of the day's offerings, offered between break of day and sunrise, so the evening sacrifice was the last, offered between the two evenings, between sunset and the end of twilight. Ezra, Clarke pictures, sat confounded in mind and distressed in soul, scarcely knowing what to do, having probably withdrawn himself into some sequestered place or secret part of the temple, spending the hours in meditation and reflection.

The other wesleyan-arminian witness, John Wesley, explains why that hour was chosen for what would follow: the evening sacrifice was when the people used to assemble together, so that his public mourning and confession would be seen and felt by many. And Wesley draws the lesson the gathering teaches — that all good people ought to own those who appear and act for God against vice and profaneness; everyone that fears God ought to stand by them and do what he can to strengthen their hands. The witnesses converge on a single picture. A man's private grief has become a public rallying-point: the tremblers at God's word, few perhaps among a careless multitude, draw together around the one who mourns, and their silent solidarity through the long afternoon is itself the first stirring of the reformation the chapter will bring. Gill marks their reverence, Keil and Delitzsch the cause of their dread, Clarke the hour and the solitary sufferer, Wesley the duty of standing with him — and together they show that the fear of God, wherever it is real, cannot look on the sins of men unmoved.
5:
The hour of prayer arrives, and the witnesses watch Ezra gather himself for it. The reformed John Gill reads "I rose up from my heaviness" as a rising from the very signs of grief — from sitting on the ground, and from his fasting, for he had eaten nothing that day, the report having reached him early in the morning. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke marks the posture that followed: he fell upon his knees in token of the deepest humility, and spread out his hands as if to lay hold on the mercy of God. John Wesley reads the same movement as a deliberate change of attitude — from the mournful posture of the astonished mourner into the posture of a petitioner — and explains again the timing: he did this at the evening sacrifice because then the devout used to come into the courts of the temple, that hearing his confession they too might be made sensible of the people's sins; and he did it with an eye to that great propitiation of which the sacrifice was a peculiar type.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry dwells longest on the time and its meaning. The evening sacrifice especially was a type of the great propitiation — that blessed Lamb of God who in the evening of the world was to take away sin by the sacrifice of himself; and Henry supposes Ezra made his confession, as it were, with his hand upon the head of that great sacrifice through which we receive the atonement. He recalls too that it was at the time of the evening sacrifice that the angel Gabriel had come to Daniel with the word concerning Messiah the Prince in Daniel 9:21, and thinks Ezra may have had regard to that in choosing the hour.

Henry traces the preparation step by step. Ezra rose up from his heaviness, shaking off so much of the burden of grief as was needful to lift up his heart to God; he fell upon his knees, putting himself into the posture of a penitent humbling himself and a petitioner suing for mercy, in both representing the people for whom he was now an intercessor; and he spread out his hands as one affected with what he was about to say, reaching out with earnest expectation for a gracious answer. What follows, Henry notes, is not strictly a prayer, for there is not a word of petition in it; it is rather the offering up of pious and devout affections to God — a penitent confession, not of his own sin from a burdened conscience, but of the sin of his people, from a gracious concern for the honour of God and the welfare of Israel, a lively picture of ingenuous repentance. The witnesses agree: before a word is spoken, the very body of the man — kneeling, hands outspread, risen from the dust of his mourning — has already begun to confess.
6:
The prayer begins with a confession of shame, and the witnesses gather around its opening words. The reformed John Gill observes that Ezra opens "O my God" in faith — that even as he sets out to confess sin and repent, he lays hold of God as his covenant God, for that prayer is right which is put up in faith, and that repentance genuine which flows from it. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke feels the weight of "I am ashamed and blush": God had been so often provoked and had so often pardoned, and the people had still transgressed, that Ezra was ashamed to come again to the throne of grace to ask mercy on their behalf — "this," Clarke adds, "is the genuine feeling of every reawakened backslider."

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch trace the train of thought the verse sets in motion: Ezra scarcely dares lift up his face to God for shame at the greatness of the people's misdeeds; from the days of the fathers God had sorely punished them, yet had lately turned his pity toward them again — and now they had transgressed afresh. The confession, they note, is that "our iniquities are increased over our head, and our trespass is grown up unto the heavens," the language of a guilt too great to be measured.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry unfolds that image and the shame that answers it. Our iniquities are increased over our heads, he paraphrases — we are ready to perish in them as in deep waters, so general is the prevalency, so violent the power, so threatening the consequences of the sin; iniquity has grown to such a height that it reaches the heavens, so impudent that it dares heaven, so provoking that, like the sin of Sodom, it cries to heaven for vengeance. Yet Henry will not leave the penitent without comfort: though their sins reach to the heavens, God's mercy is in the heavens, as Psalms 36:5 declares, and where sin abounds grace will much more abound. On the shame itself he is searching. Sin is a shameful thing, he says; holy shame is as necessary an ingredient in true repentance as holy sorrow; the sins of others should be our shame, and we should blush for those who will not blush for themselves. Penitent sinners never see so much reason to be ashamed as when they lift up their faces before God — like the publican who hung down his head in Luke 18:13. And the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley marks why Ezra says "our": he includes himself among the transgressors, both because he was conscious of his own sins and because, so many of the princes, priests, and people having done this thing, the guilt was now become national.
7:
The confession lengthens its view backward, tracing the guilt across generations. The reformed John Gill hears in "since the days of our fathers" an aggravation: the sins now lamented had been long continued in, an inheritance of transgression running down to this present day. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch spell out the punishment that guilt had drawn: for their iniquities the people, with their kings and their priests, had been delivered into the hand of the kings of the lands — to the sword, to captivity, to plunder, and to "confusion of face," the shame that covers the guilty, the same idiom that stands in Daniel 9:7. And the phrase "as it is this day" they take to mean that the suffering was not past but present: Israel was still under the yoke of foreign sovereigns even now.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the same clause to the same effect. "Have we been" means the people were not purged from the guilt of their fathers' sins but were still feeling the sad effects of them — and worse, were repeating the very sins that had brought those effects down. The past tense of judgment and the present tense of transgression meet in one sentence, so that the prayer confesses both an old debt unpaid and a new one freshly contracted.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the aggravation out fully. That the sin had been persisted in since the days of the fathers, he says, was so far from excusing it that it heightened it: we should have taken warning not to stumble at the same stone, and the corruption is so much the worse that it has taken deep root and begins to plead prescription. Nor did the great and sore judgments God had brought for their sins mend them; for their iniquities they had been delivered to the sword and to captivity, and yet were not reformed, not reclaimed — "brayed in the mortar, and yet the folly not gone," as the proverb warns in Proverbs 27:22, corrected but not reclaimed. Henry fears from this that the measure of the iniquity was nearly full. The witnesses converge: Gill on the long continuance, Keil and Delitzsch on the judgments still pressing, Wesley on the guilt unpurged and the sin renewed, Henry on a chastisement that had drawn blood but changed nothing — all confessing that a people who will not learn from a generation of suffering have no plea left but mercy.
8:
From the long night of judgment the prayer turns to a sudden dawn of favour, and the witnesses weigh every word of it. The reformed John Gill notes the sting hidden in "a little space": it was but a small time since God had first begun to show favour, so that the people's swift relapse argued a strange propensity to evil, which not even the recent goodness of God could restrain. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the phrase "for a little moment," borrowing the language of Isaiah 26:20 — a brief interval of grace set against the long ages of suffering from the days of Assyria onward; and they take the "rescued remnant" to be the new community delivered from Babylon and returned to the land, a mere remnant against the numerous population of former days.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fills in the images. The "little space" is the very interval in which they were returning from servitude; the "grace shown" is God's disposing the hearts of the Persian kings to publish edicts in their favour; the "remnant to escape" is real, for the ten tribes were gone irrecoverably and much even of Judah and Benjamin still lingered beyond the Euphrates. The "nail in his holy place" Clarke reads as even so much ground as to fix their tent-poles in; the "lightening of the eyes" as a thorough knowledge of themselves and their highest interest; and the "little reviving" as a new trial granted to a people who had been perishing — God beginning with little, to see whether they would make wise and faithful use of it. John Wesley reads the nail the same way, a metaphor from tents fastened by cords and pins, meaning some kind of settlement after being tossed from place to place; the "holy place" is Jerusalem the holy city, and the "bondage" remains, for they were not yet quite delivered, being even here in subjection to their former lords.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers these mercies into an ascending order and turns them against the sin. He marks the time — "now for a little space," so lately were they in the furnace, and none could say how soon they might return to it; the fountain — grace shown from the Lord, his free grace, without merit of theirs, though the Persian kings were the instruments; the streams — that they were not forsaken in their bondage, that a remnant was left, and that they had "a nail in his holy place," which Henry explains as the setting up of the house of God and the settling of its worship; and the effect — that it enlightened their eyes and revived their hearts, life from the dead, a little reviving that was earnest of greater. How ungrateful, then, Henry has the penitent cry, to offend a God so kind, and to mingle in sin with the very nations from whom they had been so wonderfully delivered.
9:
The prayer names the depth from which mercy had lifted them. The reformed John Gill fixes the plain confession "we were bondmen" — servants to the Chaldeans in Babylon, an admission of bondage more frank than the Jews of a later day would make of themselves. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch unfold the whole sentence: though bondmen, God had not forsaken them in their bondage but had extended mercy to them in the sight of the kings of Persia, to give them a reviving, to set up the house of their God and repair its desolations, and to give them "a wall in Judah and in Jerusalem."

Over that last figure the witnesses pause. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley takes the "wall" not as literal masonry but as the favour of the kings of Persia, whose edicts were the people's security against all the enemies that encompassed them, and the gracious providence of God which had planted them again in their own land and watched over them from time to time. It is a wall of protection rather than of stone — the royal decree and the divine care standing between a defenceless remnant and its foes.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the reviving and the rebuilt house as the sweetest of the streams of mercy. That they were not forsaken in their bondage but had, even in Babylon, the tokens of God's presence, and that they now had their religion settled and the temple service restored in a constant method — this Henry reckons a great comfort and advantage. To have stated opportunities of worshipping God is no small mercy: "Blessed are those that dwell in God's house," like Anna who departed not from the temple, and the gracious soul says of it, "this is my rest for ever." The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the humbling truth of the bondage, Keil and Delitzsch the sweep of the mercies that answered it, Wesley the wall that was really the king's favour and God's providence, Henry the restored house of prayer that crowned them all. Together they make the ninth verse the high-water mark of the prayer's gratitude — a people who were slaves, unforsaken in their slavery, and now set again in their own land with the house of God rebuilt in their midst; which only sharpens the question the next verse will ask, how such a people could sin again.
10:
Gratitude turns abruptly to self-arraignment, and the witnesses hear in the question the speechlessness of a guilty conscience. The reformed John Gill paraphrases "what shall we say after this?" as the cry of a people who can find no apology, no excuse — what can be said in favour of such ingratitude, or what kindness can be looked for by those who have behaved so basely? The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sharpens the timing that makes it so bitter: even in the midst of these first beginnings of respite and mercy, "we have begun to provoke thee anew." The sin was not a relapse after long ease but an affront offered while the very ink of deliverance was still wet.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch supply the answer the question seems to withhold. What can we say after this — after such proofs of the divine compassion as have just been rehearsed — and the only answer that can be given is the confession that follows: we can say nothing except that we have forsaken thy commandments and requited thy kindness with sins. The question is not rhetorical evasion but the doorway to a plea of guilty.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes this the very anatomy of amazement. The discoveries of guilt excite amazement, he says — the more we think of sin, the worse it looks; and the difficulty of the case excites it too, for how shall a people so circumstanced recover themselves and make their peace with God? True penitents, Henry observes, are at a loss what to say. They cannot say, We have not sinned, for that would be to deceive themselves; they cannot say, Have patience, and we will pay thee all, for God knows they are insolvent; they cannot say, There is no hope, for that would only make bad worse. Yet true penitents will consider what to say, and beg God to teach them — and Henry supplies the words: "I have sinned, I have done foolishly; God be merciful to me a sinner," after the counsel of Hosea 14:2, "take with you words, and turn to the LORD." The witnesses converge on a single note. Gill and Clarke fix the shamefaced silence, Keil and Delitzsch turn it toward confession, Henry teaches the penitent what at last to say — and all agree that the honest soul, brought to the end of its excuses, has nothing left but to plead guilty and cast itself on mercy.
11:
The prayer now sets the sin against the express word of God, and the witnesses examine the command it names. The reformed John Gill identifies "thy servants the prophets" as Moses, Joshua, and others through whom the charge had come down. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch are more precise about the citation. The words introduced by "saying" — that the land Israel went in to possess was an unclean land, defiled through the filthiness and the abominations of its peoples, who had filled it from one end to another with their uncleanness — are found in just these terms neither in the prophetic books nor in the Pentateuch; they are not, therefore, a verbal quotation but a summary declaration that the prohibition of intermarriage with the heathen had been inculcated by the prophets as by Moses. Ezra gathers the sense of the law rather than reciting a single text.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fastens on the vivid picture of the land's pollution. "Have filled it from one end to another" he reads as a flood: the abominations of the peoples had been like a sweeping, mighty torrent that increased until it filled the whole land and carried everything before it. The uncleanness was not a stain in one corner but a defilement running the length and breadth of the country, so that to marry into such nations was to wed oneself to a whole tide of corruption.

The witnesses do not divide, and together they show why Ezra reaches for the prophets. The point is not to quote chapter and verse but to establish that the thing done was done against a standing, well-known command of God, delivered again and again through his servants. Gill names the lawgivers, Keil and Delitzsch guard the exact status of the words as a faithful summary rather than a citation, Clarke paints the uncleanness the command was meant to keep Israel from. The land had been given to a holy people precisely on the condition that they not defile themselves with its former inhabitants; and by rehearsing that condition, the prayer makes plain that the marriages were no mere lapse of prudence but a breach of the covenant terms on which the whole gift of the land depended. It is one thing to break a rule of custom, another to violate the very charter of one's dwelling in the land — the very terms the next verse will spell out in the words of the prohibition itself.
12:
The command Ezra pleads is now quoted in full: give not your daughters to their sons, nor take their daughters for your sons, nor seek their peace or their wealth for ever. The reformed John Gill notes that the prohibition is of marriage, and that it stands here in the very same language as the ancient statute of Deuteronomy 7:3, which forbade Israel to give or take in marriage among the nations of Canaan. The command was no novelty but the old law of separation, repeated to a generation that had forgotten it.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch attend to the promise annexed to the prohibition and to the argument it prepares. The law bade Israel refuse these marriages and refuse to seek the welfare of these peoples, "that ye may be strong, and eat the good of the land, and leave it for an inheritance to your children for ever" — the possession of the good land being bound up with obedience to this very command. And they show how Ezra builds upon it: taking up again the "after all this" of the earlier verse, he will reason that after all God has brought upon them for their evil deeds, and after he has punished them less than their iniquities deserved and given them this rescued remnant, for them to break the command again would be to provoke God to anger "till there should be no remnant nor escaping." The prohibition, in other words, is cited not as dry law but as the hinge of a fearful argument about what a fresh breach must bring.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws out the paradox in the word "strong." Men might fancy, he says, that making leagues and marriages with their powerful neighbours was the surest way to establish themselves; but God assures them of the contrary — such alliances would weaken and ruin them, while the opposite course, keeping separate and trusting him, would make them strong. The carnal calculation and the divine promise stand exactly opposed. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the command's descent from the law of Deuteronomy, Keil and Delitzsch its promise of secure inheritance and its place in Ezra's mounting plea, Wesley the reversal by which the very policy that seemed to strengthen would in truth destroy. Together they show that the marriages Ezra mourns were not merely irregular but self-defeating — a grasping after security by the one road that God had marked out to ruin.
13:
The prayer looks back over the whole weight of chastisement and confesses that even so it had been mercy. The reformed John Gill lists what "all that is come upon us" had included — famine, sword, pestilence, and captivity, the judgments visited upon Israel for their idolatries and other heinous sins. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke seizes on the astonishing admission that follows: great, numerous, and oppressive as those calamities had been, yet merely as temporal punishments they had been much less than the people's provocations deserved. The confession does not complain that God was severe; it marvels that he was lenient.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry presses that paradox to its depth. In the judgments by which they had already smarted for their sins, he says, God had punished them less than their iniquities deserved, so that he looked upon them as still in debt upon the old account. "What!" Henry has the penitent exclaim — "and yet shall we run up a new score? Has God dealt so gently with us in correcting us, and shall we thus abuse his favour and turn his grace into wantonness?" He sets the confession beside the prophet's comfort in Isaiah 40:2, that Zion "hath received of the LORD's hand double for all her sins"; yet Ezra, out of a penitential sense of the great malignity in the sin, acknowledges the opposite — that though the punishment was very great, it was still less than they had earned.

The witnesses do not divide, and the note they strike is one of the rarest in true repentance. It is easy for the chastised to feel that God has dealt hardly with them; it is the mark of a broken and honest heart to feel, as Ezra does, that God has dealt far more gently than justice required, and that the mercy which spared them only deepens the guilt of sinning again. Gill numbers the strokes that had fallen, Clarke fixes them as temporal and light beside the desert of the sin, Henry turns the whole into a horror at the thought of adding a new debt to an old one only half-remitted. The verse thus becomes the moral pivot of the prayer: not "God has punished us too much," but "God has punished us too little for us to dare offend again" — a reckoning that leaves the penitent no ground of complaint and every reason for fear, which the next verse will voice.
14:
The confession rises now into open dread. The reformed John Gill glosses the question "should we again break thy commandments, and join in affinity with the people of these abominations?" by naming what those peoples were — nations guilty of abominable idolatries and of all uncleanness, so that to ally with them was to wed the very corruption God had judged. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch carry the sentence to its trembling conclusion: after God has spared them beyond their desert and given them this escaped remnant, were they to break his commandments again and join in affinity with the people of these abominations, would he not be angry with them "till thou hadst consumed us, so that there should be no remnant nor escaping"? The logic is inexorable — a relapse after such mercy could end only in extirpation.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the verse as the voice of a holy fear. After all the judgments that had come to reclaim them from sin, and all the deliverances wrought to engage them to God and duty, if they should again break his commandments by joining in affinity with the children of disobedience and learning their ways, what could they expect but that God should be angry till he had consumed them, and not so much as a remnant be left? And Henry draws from it a solemn general truth: "There is not a surer nor sadder presage of ruin to any people than revolting to sin, to the same sins again, after great judgments and great deliverances." Those who will be wrought upon neither by the one nor by the other, he warns, are fit to be rejected as reprobate silver, for the founder melteth in vain — the image of Jeremiah 6:29.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the abominable character of the nations, Keil and Delitzsch the arithmetic of wrath that a fresh sin must complete, Henry the pastoral warning that a people twice-schooled by judgment and deliverance and still unchanged has nothing left to look for but consuming anger. The verse is the dark bottom of the prayer: having confessed that God punished less than they deserved, Ezra now confesses that to sin again against such forbearance would leave even God's covenant patience no room to spare them. There is no plea of merit here, no bargaining — only the naked recognition that the next transgression might be the last, and that a remnant so lately rescued could, by its own folly, be swept utterly away. It is from this precipice that the closing verse will cast the whole matter upon the righteousness of God.
15:
The prayer ends not in petition but in surrender to the justice of God. The reformed John Gill reads "thou art righteous" as an acknowledgment that God would be seen to be just even should Israel be entirely cut off and utterly consumed for their iniquities — the penitent conceding the sentence before it is passed. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch catch the surprising use to which Ezra puts that righteousness. He appeals to it not, as another might, to plead for pardon, but to rouse the conscience of the people: God's righteousness had shown itself in punishing a once-numerous nation so sorely that only a small escaped remnant now survived, and to that righteousness Ezra points to show what, after this fresh relapse, they had to fear. "Behold, we are before thee in our trespasses," he prays, "for we cannot stand before thee because of this."

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke hears a gentler note in the same word. "Righteous," he says, is one of the meanings of the Hebrew that shades into "merciful" — the sense to which Paul appeals when he speaks of God declaring his righteousness for the remission of sins that are past in Romans 3:25; and it is because of this righteousness or mercy that a remnant remained escaped at all. As for "in our trespasses," Clarke takes it that the people have no righteousness of their own but are clothed and covered with their sins; and "we cannot stand before thee because of this" he sets beside the psalmist's cry, "if thou, LORD, shouldest mark iniquities, O Lord, who shall stand?" in Psalms 130:3, recalling that in the temple service the priests might stand and minister only when pure from all pollution.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley completes the posture. "We are before thee," he says, means we are here in thy presence, and so are all our sins; we are arraigning ourselves before thy tribunal, acknowledging thee to be just if thou destroy us — and "before thee," taken of judgment as the word often is, means that we must needs fall and perish at thy presence. The witnesses part ways only over the shade of that one word. Gill, Keil and Delitzsch, and Wesley fix the confession of a righteousness that could justly consume them; Clarke hears within that very righteousness the mercy that had spared a remnant. So the great prayer closes as it began, in shame and self-abasement, with no claim urged and no request framed — only a people cast, guilty and unable to stand, upon the justice and the mercy of the God they have wronged. And here, though Ezra frames no petition, the confession itself becomes the opening through which, in the next chapter, the covenant of reformation will be made.
